Endpoint Testing with Supertest

Sending real HTTP-shaped requests into the exported app, without starting a server or binding a port.

A unit test calling getTicketById directly never touches routing, middleware, or status codes — it can't tell you whether GET /tickets/:id is actually wired up correctly. For that you need a request to genuinely go through Express, the way a real client's would. Supertest does exactly that: it wraps an Express app object and lets a test send it .get()/.post() requests, in-process, and inspect the real response — status code, JSON body, headers — that comes back.

The reason this is possible without a running server at all is the app.js/server.js split from earlier this lesson: app.js only ever builds and exports the app, and server.js is the one file that calls app.listen(...). A test can import the exported app directly and hand it straight to Supertest, skipping server.js — and the port — entirely.

// Figure 1.15: endpoint-testing the API (tests/integration/tickets.routes.test.js, excerpt)
import request from 'supertest';
import app from '../../src/app.js';

describe('GET/POST /tickets', () => {
  it('GET /tickets returns the seeded list', async () => {
    const res = await request(app).get('/tickets');

    expect(res.status).toBe(200);
    expect(Array.isArray(res.body)).toBe(true);
  });

  it('POST /tickets without a subject returns 400', async () => {
    const res = await request(app)
      .post('/tickets')
      .send({ description: 'Missing subject' });

    expect(res.status).toBe(400);
  });
});

request(app).get('/tickets') returns a Promise resolving to a response object — familiar shape, same async/await as everywhere else in this lesson. The second test is the more interesting one: it never calls createTicket directly, it POSTs a body that's missing subject and checks that the whole pipeline — routing, the controller's manual validation, the response it sends — actually produces a 400, exactly as REST's use of status codes as part of the contract (this lesson's REST topic) promises it should.

That's the difference from the previous slide's unit test in one sentence: this one is checking that all the pieces fit together through the real interface, not that one function returns the right value in isolation. Both kinds of test already pass against the code you've built this week — a habit this project keeps up, and grows, through every week from here on.
